The core idea is to replace the fixed temperature in the energy score with a temperature parameter that is learned and adaptive to the input. This learned temperature is implemented as a single fully connected layer that takes the penultimate layer's output as input and produces a single scalar per input, which is then passed through a Batch Normalization layer and a sigmoid activation to normalize it to the range (0, 1). The authors argue that this adaptive temperature allows for a more nuanced control of the OOD score, leading to improved detection performance. The method is evaluated across a range of tasks, including image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, demonstrating its versatility and effectiveness. The empirical results show that AbeT consistently outperforms several baseline OOD detection methods, including those based on maximum softmax probability (MSP), ODIN, and the standard energy score. The authors also provide some insights into how the model learns to distinguish between in-distribution and OOD samples, suggesting that the learned temperature plays a crucial role in this process. The paper's contribution lies in the novel combination of a learned temperature with the energy score and the empirical demonstration of its effectiveness across various tasks. While the paper presents a compelling empirical case for the proposed method, it lacks a rigorous theoretical analysis and a comprehensive evaluation on some of the most challenging OOD detection benchmarks.
